May I cheat on this answer?

Umineko no Naku Koro ni (When the Seagulls Cry)

Now, this is what is called a Visual Novel, which is sort of a game, but mostly not. It's almost entirely straight up reading - it has no real gameplay or choices to make, it's just words to read and it's supported by pictures and music. (And it has an absolutely incredible soundtrack.

It is eight "books" long, and each one takes quite a long time to read. The first one only takes about maybe 4-6 hours, but each following book is about 2-4 hours longer than the last, and yes, that means the final book is indeed obscenely long.

It starts off with what appears to be a typical murder mystery - rich family gathers for their annual family conference and people turn up dead in a closed room. But then a mysterious letter shows up, seemingly out of thin air, sent from one claiming to be a witch. The letter claims that all of the residents of the mansion on the island, trapped within a typhoon with no escape, will all be sacrificed on that night for her revival. Some believe in the mysterious 19th person on the island which should only have 18, the witch Beatrice, and others believe that the culprit must be one of the remaining human residents of the mansion. But as the murders become more and more grotesque, and more and more seemingly impossible to be performed with human tricks, will the remaining family members and servants cave in and believe in the witch? Is magic real, or not? Will they solve the crime, or will they all die? When the seagulls that enliven the docks return after the storm, when the seagulls cry, will anyone be left alive?

The story has more twists and turns than you can imagine, and the character development is absolutely phenomenal. I may not be the most versed in literature, but I'll be damned if Umineko is not the best thing I've ever read in my life.

You can download a "demo" (the entire first novel) for free (legally) via the translation group's website. It's unofficial, but fully endorsed by the creator of the series.

There was also an anime but it was a complete and total bastardization and is panned by everyone who has ever touched the visual novel. It also only covers the first half since it sold so poorly (because it was bad) they never made a second season.

And yes, if the name sounds familiar to you, it is indeed a spiritual successor to Higurashi no Naku Koro ni, which also got an anime and was very popular several years back (which is also a shitty adaptation, but nobody knew since the VN for Higurashi wasn't translated back then). They just released a remastered version of the first chapter of Higurashi on Steam recently too. But it's not really required to read in order to enjoy Umineko (though it is recommended.)

Sorry if I kinda went off on a tangent here, but it bugs me that more people don't know of this wonderful story.

Mindfulness has lost its Buddhist roots, and it may not be doing you good

The author of this article is Miguel Farias. His citation for his startling claim that "we are no closer to finding out how meditation works" is a link to his own book, given positive reviews by colleagues and such. Do we trust this claim, whose only proof provided is something we must purchase to verify?

The second, and most important thing to note, is the primary claim and study refers only to "Individuals with a history of recurrent depression have a high risk of repeated depressive relapse or recurrence." These individuals would be classified medically as having "treatment resistant depression", often combined with PTSD (or recurring cute form, ASD). Individuals with chronic stress disorders, or chronic acute recurring episodes, are a very small subset of a large problem. Often these individuals have permanent neurological alteration that triggers these episodes, whose symptoms can only be mitigated and not prevented. Therefore it is of no surprise that other therapies, if they have any success, would only have success to the extent any other therapy can. Very little.

However, it is less clear how powerful and long-lasting these changes are [...]

This is not true. There are various studies showing neurological changes with different practices in the same regions that grow in "strength" over time. Comparison studies with groups who practice various yogas, zen or contemplative meditation, all show different results on the mind. The most common one is a stronger effect on the neo-cortex which exerts "control" over autonomous functions and responses. I'd link examples but they're all over pubmed - the topic and use of fMRI is very popular.

What matters more than fMRI and related studies, however, are the results of these changes. These have been studied, primarily, through self reporting in studies like this. In general the effects of these neurological changes are antagonist to dysfunctional behavior triggered by self induced anxiety.

The further note of its "possible negative effects" seems to coyly gloss over the fact that the entirety of those effects stem, not from healthy people, but from already severely dysfunctional individuals. There are a number of cases, primarily with psychosis, where the same processes of meditation (introspection or contemplation) could exacerbate the condition. This is exactly what the study linked shows, but not what the blog writer states. He uses fear-inducing language instead, even though there's really little to be concerned about unless you're presenting with psychosis and paranoia. The study is specifically relating to the ethics and need for careful screening to prevent these persons from possibly worsening their condition by practicing this unguided introspection. Which, to no surprise, worsens negative thought patterns by the individual contemplating those thoughts.

My final judgement is this is a very poorly written article, which does not express with honesty the current state of research, nor clearly states how the whole of his proof applies, explicitly, to a very small minority of the mentally ill. His linking to his own book alone as proof for a broad over-reaching statement, which again only applies to a minority of the mentally ill, invokes a sensation of disgust with his ethics.
